Treating the image as a matrix where red pixels are assigned value \(a\) and white pixels value \(b\), this partitions the matrix into three constant-value blocks (with the cross interrupting the canton). A matrix composed of three such rectangular constant blocks can be expressed as a sum of three rank-1 matrices (one per region), so its rank is at most 3. Thus the maximal possible rank is 3.

Rewrite  
\[
M = a\cdot\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top - (a-b)\sum_{k=1}^4 u_k v_k^\top,
\]  
where each term \(u_k v_k^\top\) is the indicator matrix of one of the four rectangular white regions created by subtracting the cross from the canton. Consequently \(M\) is a linear combination of five rank-1 matrices.  

The four rectangles are delimited by only two distinct row intervals and two distinct column intervals inside the canton. The five generating vectors therefore lie in a vector space of dimension at most 4, so  
\[
\rank(M)\le 4.
\]  
By choosing the heights and widths of the canton and cross so that the two row-interval indicators are linearly independent from each other and from the all-ones vector (and likewise for the column indicators), the bound is attained. Hence the maximal possible rank is exactly 4.

\]  
The four spanning vectors are linearly independent for any choice of column indices that realize the geometric containment relations of the flag (canton strictly contains both arms of the cross, and the two arms have distinct widths). Hence the row space of \(M\) has dimension exactly 4 whenever \(a\neq b\). No larger rank is possible, because every row of \(M\) is necessarily a linear combination of those four vectors.  

Thus the maximal attainable rank is 4.
